title: How to find out who owns an LLC
summary: A state registry often shows little more than that an LLC was formed and who receives its legal papers.
body_markdown:
Search the registry of the state where the LLC was formed and read the documents it has filed, because some states ask for managers or members in the formation filing or a periodic report and others record little beyond the registered agent. Then look where the LLC leaves names as it does business: deeds and mortgages, UCC financing statements, court cases, assumed-name filings, licences and, if it raised money, a Form D with the SEC. Treat each name as a lead until a second, independent record agrees, because a signature shows who acts for the LLC, which is not always who owns it.


Sometimes. California's Statement of Information lists an LLC's managers, or each member if it has no managers, and Texas records an LLC's initial managers or members and receives a yearly report of its managers, and of its members if it is member-managed. Delaware's free search shows little more than the name, file number, formation date and registered agent, and its LLCs file no annual report. In California the operating agreement is kept by the LLC and not filed with the secretary of state.


Members are the owners: the IRS says the owners of an LLC are called members, and they can be people, corporations, other LLCs or foreign entities. A manager runs the LLC and may or may not be a member. In a member-managed LLC the members run it themselves, so a filing that lists them is listing owners, while a manager-managed LLC's filings may name only its managers.


Not necessarily. The registered agent is the person or company that accepts legal papers for the LLC, and an LLC can name a commercial agent, a business that provides the service to other companies. In a small LLC the agent is sometimes a member or manager, so the name is worth checking against other records, but it is not evidence of ownership on its own.


Treat the parent as a new search. Find the state where it was formed, read its filings there and in any state where it is registered to do business, and look for the people who sign its deeds, liens and assumed-name statements. Record each link with its source, and stop when the chain reaches a person or a record that names no one, because a person who signs for every layer is a strong lead but has not been shown to own them.


Search the LLC's name at the county recorder, where deeds and mortgages are indexed by the names of the parties, and open the documents. A mortgage or deed of trust the LLC signed names the person who signed for it, and the notary's acknowledgement names the person who appeared, while the county's tax records can show where the bill is sent. Then check that person or address against the LLC's state filings, because the signer may be a manager or an agent rather than an owner.
